name: Gilbert's Dimple Machine

card.summary: A 1920s spring-bow brace with pointed knobs that pressed dents into the cheeks, marketed to give wearers dimples and now revived as a curiosity online.
card.aka: Dimple Digger; Isabella Gilbert dimple maker; Dimple Maker
card.note: Vintage novelty; the AMA reportedly warned about it, and lasting results are unknown.

quick.overview:
The Dimple Machine was a face-worn device invented by Evangeline Isabella Gilbert of Rochester, New York. A patent was filed in 1921 and granted in 1926. Two pointed knobs on a spring bow pressed into the cheeks, and the idea was that sustained pressure would leave dimples.

Dimples are valued as a charming facial feature, and cosmetic dimple surgery exists today. The machine is a historic non-surgical attempt at the same look; it was worn overnight, and whether any results lasted is unknown.
quick.how: The wearer fitted the brace to the face so the knobs sat on the cheeks, tightened it with screws on the improved model, and wore it for a period, reportedly overnight. A chin fitting was added later.
quick.risks: The American Medical Association reportedly warned that frequent users could develop cancer, and pressure on skin carries bruising and irritation concerns. It is mainly a historical novelty.

lead: Gilbert's Dimple Machine was a device invented by Evangeline Isabella Gilbert of Rochester, New York, who filed a patent in 1921 that was granted in 1926 [1].

The early version had two pointed knobs fixed to a spring bow that pressed into the cheeks; an improved version added a fitting for a chin dimple and screws to increase pressure [1]. It was meant to be worn overnight so dimples would appear [2].

It belongs to a line of dimple-making gadgets: Martin Goetze's 1896 device used an ivory knob and a rotating cylinder, and the Dolly Dimpler was advertised in 1924 [1][2]. Images of the machine from 1936 circulated in Modern Mechanix, and it has drawn renewed attention on social media as a vintage curiosity.

infobox: Two knobs on a spring bow; later chin fitting and tightening screws [1]

paras: The first model pressed two pointed knobs into the cheeks via a spring bow. The improved model added a chin attachment and screws to tighten the pressure for a deeper effect [1]. Dimples themselves are thought to relate to a double or bifid zygomaticus major muscle [3].

Gilbert filed in 1921, and the patent was granted in 1926 [1]. A 1936 image of the machine appeared in Modern Mechanix [1]. Earlier, Martin Goetze's 1896 hand-drill-like device softened skin around an ivory knob, and the Dolly Dimpler was advertised in Motion Picture Magazine in August 1924 [1][2]. Surgical dimple creation, dimpleplasty, became available from the 1960s [3].
No studies found. It is unknown whether the machine produced lasting dimples, and the AMA is reported to have warned that frequent users could develop cancer [3].
